endorsements.quote: Someone must remain answerable when a tool shapes decisions in serious illness, and two accountability problems are specific to this field, both of which are sharpest as the illness advances.

Around these sit the general duties that this population makes acute: a named accountable owner, the correct regulatory class under the European Union’s AI Act, and post-deployment monitoring for drift and for any signal of hastened death, because casemix and pathways shift over time [ 21 , 22 , 44 ]; embedding responsible-AI practices from the outset helps anticipate and resolve the ethical issues these tools raise [ 45 ].

Co-design in palliative care is feasible and improves relevance: a remote-monitoring system co-designed with patients and health workers, and a symptom app co-created through community-partnered participatory research, were both judged usable by their intended users, and sustained involvement is possible even among older adults often assumed to be disengaged [ 27 , 28 , 29 ].
Report age, frailty, multimorbidity, ethnicity, diagnosis and setting versus the target.
Analyse whether the outcome label encodes existing under-referral rather than true need.

unlisted_practices: Tie every AI output to an actionable palliative response, not to a bare prognosis or number.
Use goal-concordance rather than survival or cost as the AI target.
Design AI tools so that saved clinician time is routed back to the bedside and automation never displaces the clinician from the patient and family.
Design AI so its prognosis prediction does not silently trigger withdrawal of treatment (self-fulfilling prophecy safeguard).
Ensure AI-inferred preferences never displace documented wishes or the surrogate.
Require explicit clinician authorisation and reversible, audited actions before AI initiates or withdraws an end-of-life pathway.
Validate palliative AI on goal-concordant care, quality of life and symptom burden rather than accuracy alone.
Handle missing-not-at-random data near end of life explicitly and govern decedent and family data lawfully.
Make disclosure norms and spiritual framing in AI tools configurable rather than hard-coded.
Monitor deployed palliative AI for drift and for hastened-death signals.
Set AI error thresholds so errors fail toward the patient's goals rather than toward escalation or withdrawal.

screen.reason: The paper introduces the PALLI-AI framework, an evidence-informed checklist and guideline for designing, reporting, and governing AI tools in palliative and end-of-life care.
